title: India Gate Goes Beyond Basmati: KRBL Bets on Poha to Win the NRI Pantry
excerpt: The world's largest basmati exporter is pushing into ready-to-cook staples like poha, vermicelli and makhana — a move that could reshape what fills diaspora kitchen shelves.
body:
For decades, the blue India Gate sack of basmati rice has been a fixture in diaspora pantries from Edison to East London — shorthand for the long-grain rice that anchors every biryani and pulao. Now its maker, KRBL, is reaching for a bigger slice of the desi kitchen, and the first move is a humble one: poha.

**Beyond the rice sack**

On June 23, KRBL announced it is launching poha — the flattened-rice breakfast staple — under the India Gate brand, framed explicitly as a push to expand in the broader staples category. The product debuts in a 500g pack through general trade and standalone modern-trade outlets, with extensions into Indori poha and other regional variants already planned, and a wider rollout into organized retail to follow.

Crucially, management has signaled this is just the opening. The company is evaluating other staple categories — vermicelli and makhana among them — that share three appealing traits: a largely unorganized market, healthy gross margins, and room for a trusted brand to consolidate a fragmented field. Basmati still makes up roughly 95 per cent of KRBL's revenue, so the diversification is less about replacing rice than building the next leg of growth on the credibility rice earned.

**Context and background**

The timing reflects a broader reality: Indian food is now the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, and the U.S. ethnic-food market is estimated in the tens of billions of dollars. That demand has lifted an entire generation of branded desi staples. Truly Indian, backed by ADF Foods, has expanded to more than 1,300 U.S. stores since launching in 2024, selling frozen samosas, low-glycemic naans and ready-to-eat meals. Its naan and chutney lines were named 2026 NEXTY finalists at Natural Products Expo West — a sign that authentic Indian staples are no longer niche imports but recognized players in mainstream natural-foods retail.

KRBL's export business has had a turbulent stretch, with basmati shipments rattled by regional conflict and volatile trade. Building a portfolio of shelf-stable staples is partly insurance — a way to lean on the India Gate name across more aisles and more occasions than the dinner plate alone.

**Current developments**

Poha is a shrewd entry point. It is fast, forgiving and beloved across regions, the kind of dish a time-pressed NRI can put together on a weekday morning when dosa batter feels like too much work. A reliable, consistent branded poha solves a real diaspora pain point: the inconsistency of loose, bulk-bin flattened rice that can turn to mush or stay stubbornly hard. Indori poha — the sev-topped, fennel-scented Madhya Pradesh version — as a named variant shows KRBL understands that regional specificity, not generic "Indian," is what wins loyalty now.

**Diaspora impact**

For NRIs, the move means more of the everyday Indian pantry arriving pre-vetted under names they already trust. The diaspora shopper who once hunted across three ethnic stores for a decent poha or a clean makhana may soon find them stacked beside the familiar basmati. It also nudges Indian grocery retail further into the organized, branded era — better packaging, clearer labeling, more predictable quality — even as it raises the perennial diaspora debate about whether convenience flattens the character of foods that were always meant to be a little personal.

**What's next**

Watch for India Gate vermicelli and makhana to follow if the poha launch lands, and for the staples push to reach export markets where the brand already has shelf space and diaspora goodwill. If KRBL succeeds, the blue sack of rice may soon be just one item in a much larger India Gate basket — and the desi pantry abroad a little more branded, and a little more convenient, than the one the last generation carried over.
